t: 3732 - Maximum Product of Three Elements After One Replacement
o:
We must replace exactly one element with any value in [-1e5, 1e5], then pick three elements maximizing their product. Since the replacement value can be anything in range, the only useful replacements are +1e5 and -1e5 (replacing with anything else is dominated). After inserting v = ±1e5 and deleting one original element, the best triple containing v uses the best (or worst) pair among the remaining elements. Because we freely choose which element to delete and n ≥ 3, any pair of original elements leaves a third index available for the replacement.

Example 1: [-5,7,0] — with v = -1e5, the minimum pair product is -5·7 = -35, giving 3.5e6. Example 2: with v = +1e5, the maximum pair product is (-4)(-3) = 12, giving 1.2e6. Example 3: all pair products are 0, so the answer is 0.
k: Only replacement values ±1e5 can be optimal
Answer = 1e5 · max(|best pair product|, |worst pair product|) of the original array
Best pair = max(top-two product, bottom-two product); worst pair = min(bottom-two product, min·max)

a.i: Sort a copy. The maximum pair product is max(a[0]·a[1], a[-1]·a[-2]); the minimum pair product is min(a[0]·a[1], a[0]·a[-1]). Multiplying the larger absolute value by 1e5 yields the answer, since v = ±1e5 lets us pick the favorable sign.
s: Compute maxPair = max(a[0]*a[1], a[-1]*a[-2]) and minPair = min(a[0]*a[1], a[0]*a[-1])
a.sp: O(n) — sorted copy (or O(1) if sorting in place is allowed)

a.i: Track the three largest and two smallest values in a single scan; the same pair formulas then run in O(n) without sorting.
s: Scan once maintaining max1≥max2≥max3 and min1≤min2
maxPair = max(max1*max2, min1*min2); minPair = min(min1*min2, min1*max1)
a.t: O(n) — single scan with constant work per element

w: Prefer the one-pass version in interviews for O(n) time. Key correctness argument to voice: exactly one replacement means the final triple contains at most one artificial value, and choosing which index to replace is free, so pair statistics of the original array suffice. Pitfalls: returning an int (products reach 1e5 · 1e10 = 1e15 — must be 64-bit / safe in JS doubles), and forgetting the min·max candidate for the worst pair. Follow-up: allow k replacements, or ask for the replacement achieving the optimum.
